meta.title: Texas property tax, 12 days of posts
meta.subject: Texas property taxes — Gov. Abbott's plan to eliminate school property taxes, appraisal caps, the $3,000 savings claim, local government budgets
meta.subtitle: Oct 6 to Oct 17, 2026. Each dot is one post with 1K+ views about Texas property tax, plus every post repeating an earlier one, in the lane for what it argues. Higher and bigger means more views. White means 90% or more the same words as an earlier post, with a white line back to it. Coloured lines link a post to the post it quoted or replied to. Updated daily.

lanes.label: Who pays if taxes eliminated?
lanes.description: Questions or warnings that eliminating school property taxes means the state must replace the revenue, via other taxes, a state income tax, or a tax shift, with doubts about whether the savings math works.

lanes.label: Local governments erase the relief
lanes.description: Argues that cities, counties and school districts raise rates, budgets and bonds, wiping out state tax cuts, so locals need to be reined in or voted out.

lanes.label: Caps and cuts hurt services
lanes.description: Warns that tighter appraisal and revenue caps and eliminating school taxes would starve parks, public safety, health care and schools of funding.

lanes.label: Abbott's promise is election-year spin
lanes.description: Argues Abbott has had 12 years and GOP majorities yet property taxes keep rising, so the elimination plan and savings claims are misleading politics timed to the ballot.

lanes.label: GOP delivers tax relief, Dems raise
lanes.description: Claims Republicans cut property taxes (largest cut in history, homeowner relief, ending perpetual rent to the state) while Democrats like Hinojosa voted for higher taxes and an income tax.

lanes.label: Property taxes make Texas unaffordable
lanes.description: Everyday-cost frame: high property tax bills, insurance, appraisals and rents squeeze owners and renters, undercutting the 'no income tax' low-cost Texas story.

lanes.label: Pushback
lanes.description: Posts doubting, mocking, fact-checking or arguing against the dominant framings.

posts.name: Anttsinc
posts.text:
The property tax bill alone on this foreclosure is $12,000 a year—that’s $1,000 a month out of your pocket before you pay a single dime toward the actual mortgage. 

🏛️💸 That is exactly what you are signing on the dotted line for when you buy a house like this.

I've been coming out to monitor this foreclosure property since December, and the neighborhood dynamics tell you everything you need to know. Next door, someone is running an active, unpermitted mechanic business right on the street—constantly working on cars and currently blocking the driveway to this house. On the other side, it's packed with H1B visa workers dressed in full traditional foreign clothing, standing outside loudly talking in their language and staring at me every time I pull up. 🚗👀

People see these foreclosure videos and think it’s easy money, but let’s look at the harsh reality of this 4,000 sq ft house. In the Texas climate, you have to run the AC all summer long just to control the humidity. If the foundation gets damp, the moisture destroys everything. Because this house has had the electricity shut off since I took it over in December, the humidity did its worst: all the wood floors are completely ruined. They expanded, creased, warped, and the whole downstairs has to be ripped out. 🪵❌

The kitchen and bathrooms are frozen in 2002—we’re talking original linoleum and cheap wood-wrapped countertops that most buyers would immediately gut. The upstairs carpet is stained, filthy, and ruined. The entire interior needs a full paint job.

With today's interest rates, a mortgage on a home in this price tier is easily going to run you between $3,000 and $4,000 a month. Add that to the $1,000 a month tax bill, and you are easily dumping six figures into this house just to make it livable. That is the real cost of a "deal." 

👇 Would you take on a project with these neighborhood dynamics, or is it an immediate pass? Let me know below.
#ForeclosureReality #TexasRealEstate #FixerUpper #HousingMarket #CostOfHomeownership #RealEstateInvesting #anttsinc

posts.name: State Representative David Lowe
posts.text:
Texas should not routinely collect billions more than it needs. Instead of using excess revenue to grow spending, we should focus on collecting less from taxpayers in the first place.

My Texas Working Families Tax Relief Act is one piece of that strategy. It would eliminate sales taxes on everyday necessities families actually need, including car seats, school supplies, children’s clothing, safety equipment, and other essentials.

Property tax relief remains critically important, but not every Texan owns a home. Texans who rent pay taxes too, and they should also benefit when the state has the ability to reduce the tax burden.

This bill is not intended to compete with property tax relief. It is about reducing the amount of money flowing into the Texas state budget by letting working families keep more of their own money.

The current list is only a starting point. I’m willing to accept amendments on the House floor to expand this bill and provide additional tax relief.

Texas doesn’t need to find new ways to spend every available dollar. We need to collect less in the first place.

posts.name: AcmeAcres.us
posts.text:
Counties inflate what your land is worth, sell bonds against the inflated number, and refuse to hear you when you say the number is wrong.

Texas school districts print the phrase unlimited tax into their general obligation bonds. Those bonds get repaid out of property tax.

The collateral underneath them is an appraisal.

Property owners in Denton County took the appraisal method itself to court. Their argument was that the district set values to hit a budget instead of valuing the property in front of it.

They were told to protest one parcel at a time, through an appraisal review board that cannot rule on a district-wide method.

The courts decided procedure. The merits never got heard. The evidence was never ruled false and the practice was never ruled lawful.

The plaintiffs put the school bond buildout sitting on top of those valuations at 5.1 trillion dollars nationally, roughly 606 billion of it in Texas.

Case 26-179 now asks the Supreme Court whether a process that cannot grant relief can be the only door you are allowed to knock on.

I hold the deed to my place. The county holds a lien on it. Whoever holds the second one decides how long I keep the first.

Your rancher,
Jason Hanley | 208-714-0478
